title: CinderWave Systems interoperability orientation
summary: Introductory partner discovery oriented on hybrid GPU orchestration, integration touchpoints for Redwood runtime, security/compliance and pilot framing. Customer is interested in private VPC/on-prem options and automated routing between cloud and on-prem GPUs. Main blockers: network peering, KMS integration, and performance benchmarking cadence.
action_items: Alicia Gomez: Share current infra diagram + VPC peering config by 2029-01-25
Priya Patel (Redwood SE): Draft initial benchmark plan and list of test prompts by 2029-01-23
Samir Rao: Provide SOC2 audit summary & KMS architecture notes by 2029-01-24
next_steps: Redwood to send pilot checklist + security pack link
Schedule 1-hr benchmark run with CinderWave test cluster (target week of 2029-01-29)
Follow-up meeting to confirm network architecture and test dataplane (2029-01-26 proposed)
Customer to provision staging nodes and provide SSH jump host info
transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2029-01-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jonah Ruiz (Redwood Solutions Eng); Alicia Gomez, Ben Park, Mina Cho, Samir Rao (CinderWave)

00:00 Alicia: alright everyone, thanks for carving out time, i know it's late for some of us but excited to get into the weeds here.
00:12 Morgan: yeah thanks, appreciate it. quick intro, i'm Morgan, AE on the partnership team, with Priya and Jonah from eng. we'll try to keep this practical — want to map integration points and blockers.
00:25 Priya: hi all, Priya here. i'll mostly focus on runtime details, perf and the pilot plan.
00:31 Ben: cool. for context, CinderWave runs a hybrid scheduler that spans our AZ and on-prem colo racks. we have NVLink topologies in colos and A100 and newer Ampere class in cloud. our big ask is: can Redwood route requests to the best fit GPU (cost vs latency) without double-moving data?
00:52 Jonah: great, so smart routing is something we've built with policy layers. can i ask about your KV cache and model variants? are you planning to use a single model artifact across envs?
01:05 Mina: we have two main artifacts — a trimmed 7b optimized for latency in-cloud and a quantized 13b we use in on-prem nodes for throughput. the 13b uses INT8 with some custom kernels, which is where we worry about compatibility.
01:22 Priya: ah okay. custom kernel footprints and quantization profiles are typical friction. Redwood's runtime supports multiple quantized paths but we sometimes need to compile with specific kernel backends for on-prem GPUs. do you run a common libcudnn stack or are you on mixed driver versions?
01:40 Ben: mixed — colos are at 535.x drivers, some legacy colo racks are still at 510.x due to vendor firmware.
01:50 Priya: that'll matter. our compilation/kernels selector tries to pick a compatible kernel set but if the driver differences are wide we recommend packaging a small shim to ensure consistent symbol versions.
02:03 Samir: security is my lane — couple things: we need KMS integration (HSM preferred), SSO/SAML for admin, RBAC separation by team, and audit logs we can ship into our Splunk instance. do you have pointers?
02:18 Morgan: yes — we have Private mode that supports customer-managed KMS integrations and an audit export. i'll send the security pack after the call. but quick Q: do you need FIPS endpoints or an HSM-backed signer for token issuance?
02:34 Samir: we prefer HSM-backed for key wrapping, FIPS optional but nice to have.
02:40 Priya: noted. our private deploy supports KMS via standard KMIP or cloud KMS; HSM path is supported in the on-prem kit but requires a config step.
02:50 Alicia: ok great. on the routing side, latency matters for < 100ms user-facing flows; the backend batch jobs can accept higher latency. idea is to route interactive queries to nearby cloud GPUs and burst heavier loads to colo when cost-optimizing. how do you measure the tradeoffs?
03:08 Jonah: we use per-route policies (latency SLO + unit cost threshold) and fallbacks. we also do automated prefix caching to avoid recomputing KV for repeated prefixes. real question: how intrusive is cache warm-up in your flows — will we need to change model serving patterns?
03:26 Mina: worth calling out — our current app does an incremental convo state store and we append to the KV for long-living chats. we worry about KV sync across clusters.
03:38 Priya: RW has two concepts: KV persistence and prefix/KV cache. for cross-cluster sync we can surface a small sync agent or rely on shared object storage. the sync agent approach is lower latency but requires a secure channel between sites.
03:54 Ben: what's the latency bump on that? like 50ms, 200ms?
04:01 Priya: depends on distance. within same metro colo to cloud region maybe 20–60ms; cross-continent obviously more. For interactive flows we recommend colocating the cache.
04:12 Alicia: hmm. might be hard for us to colocate for every region. could we do a staged pilot to measure end-to-end?
04:19 Morgan: absolutely. proposed pilot: week-long benchmark with sample traffic, Redwood runs orchestrated routing + our autoscaler configured to your pool. we capture latency P99, cost per token, and functional correctness for prompt sets you supply.
04:33 Ben: timeline? we'd like results in two weeks if possible.
04:36 Morgan: we can target that — Priya, Jonah, thoughts?
04:40 Priya: yes, we can do an initial smoke in week 1 and a heavier run week 2. i'll draft a benchmark plan and the prompt set we need.
04:49 Jonah: i'll prepare the runbook for provisioning staging nodes and the expected metrics.
04:55 Alicia: from security side, we'll need the SOC2 summary and the endpoint for audit logs. Samir will share the baseline.
05:04 Samir: i'll upload the audit summary to the shared drive after this call.
05:10 Morgan: perfect. quick note on deployment variants: Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved pools if you want predictable throughput, while Private is more about your control plane running on your VPC or on-prem. which direction are you leaning?
05:24 Ben: early on we want private control plane in our VPC with on-prem serving nodes. may eventually look at Dedicated for high-volume tenant customers.
05:33 Priya: that maps well. Private control plane plus customer-managed serving nodes is a common pattern. two engineering notes: 1) the control plane needs peering to reach your staging API endpoints; 2) the serving nodes need outbound connectivity for health checks unless you run an air-gapped variant.
05:49 Mina: we want to avoid outbound egress from our secure racks — air-gapped is preferred for Prod; staging can have limited egress.
05:57 Priya: we have an air-gapped package, but it changes how we ship metrics/traces. we can stage with limited egress and then do a controlled cutover.
06:06 Ben: good. a few more nitty-gritty: model version pinning and rollbacks — we need safe rollbacks and canary policy support. how are rollouts handled?
06:18 Jonah: we support canary percent rollouts and automatic fallback to a pinned variant on error. rollbacks are immediate by API and viewable in the console.
06:27 Alicia: do you capture token-level cost breakdowns? we need per-tenant visibility.
06:33 Morgan: yes, Redwood Console gives per-route and per-model token breakdowns and can be filterable by tenant tag.
06:40 Samir: on compliance: you'll need to support SSO with our identity provider (we use Okta).
06:46 Morgan: SSO via SAML/SCIM is supported; we'll share the SAML metadata and provisioning docs.
06:53 Mina: on the kernel compatibility: our vendor uses a custom fused kernel for the quantized 13b that is not standard. what's the process if Redwood can't run that kernel out-of-box?
07:06 Priya: two options: 1) we compile the runtime against your kernel — requires access to the kernel artifacts and some validation, or 2) you provide a compatible model variant (e.g., a slightly different quant build) we can run with our supported kernels. Option 1 is possible but adds 1–2 weeks for validation.
07:25 Ben: do we need to share binary kernel blobs? that's a red flag for IP for some vendors.
07:30 Priya: we can work with a hashed signature and a sealed validation env. sometimes customers prefer to do the compile step themselves with our patch set.
07:40 Samir: we'd prefer to avoid shipping kernel blobs out. is there a documented path where we build with Redwood's patches internally?
07:48 Priya: yes, we have a documented on-prem build with a patch bundle and test harness. we'll put that link in the follow-up.
07:56 Morgan: ok, practical ask: Alicia — can you share your infra diagram and VPC peering notes? that'll let Priya scope the shim and benchmark footprint.
08:05 Alicia: yes i'll email the diagrams after the call.
08:10 Ben: regarding telemetry — we want traces with skimmable traces per request. do you export to open telemetry?
08:16 Jonah: we support OTLP and can export spans to your collector; we also emit per-token traces in debug mode but that increases telemetry volume.
08:26 Mina: understood. we'll start with aggregated metrics and enable request traces only for failed cases.
08:32 Priya: performance note — if you expect sub-100ms P99 we should avoid cross-cluster KV fetches. the pilot will quantify.
08:41 Ben: also curious about quantization accuracy regressions — how do you validate output fidelity across quantized variants?
08:48 Priya: we run prompt-level evals and compare token-level deltas and BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics for deterministic tasks. we'll also run your customer-specific test set.
08:58 Alicia: sounds good. anything else for the pilot scope?
09:03 Morgan: action items recap — we'll send the security pack, Priya will send the benchmark plan and required prompt sets, Jonah will send runbook, Alicia will provide infra docs, Samir will drop audit summary.
09:15 Alicia: yes. and one more — pricing model. do you have partner discounts or reserved pool pricing for integrators?
09:24 Morgan: we have reserved capacity contracts and partner pricing, will include a pilot pricing sheet. not negotiation today, but we'll share the numbers.
09:32 Ben: competitor question — we evaluated TitanCloud earlier; what would be the key Reddit differences? (laugh)
09:40 Morgan: haha, main difference: Redwood is production-first runtime with a unified API across hosted/dedicated/private and stronger observability and routing controls. we'll put a short comparison in the follow-up.
09:52 Mina: last tactical: can we get a POC NDA? our legal team needs one before we share certain artifacts.
09:57 Morgan: yes — i'll loop in our legal.
10:00 Morgan: anything else?
10:03 Alicia: no, that's it for now. thanks everyone.
10:07 Morgan: thanks — we'll follow up with the checklist and links.

(There is some crosstalk and intermittent note-taking noise between 10:10 and 12:00; audio section contains a few mis-transcribed words like 'kayvee' for KV cache and 'ampere class' rendered as 'ampir class')

End of transcript.
